item.title: Snow will vanish forever from East Africa’s iconic mountain peaks
item.description: The glacier retreat on Mt Kenya, Kilimanjaro in northern Tanzania and Rwenzori is unprecedented, says an expert.
item.content:encoded:
East Africa’s shrinking mountain glaciers on three peaks in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania will soon be no more. The 2025 State of the Climate in Africa report (page 13) estimates that the ice areas on Mt Kenya, the continent’s second-highest peak, have shrunk 96% in the past 115 years. The ice cap will cease to exist in three to five years, says the report. Rainer Prinz, who studies climate-glacier relationships, explains the intricate processes behind the retreat and what the consequences will be.

What makes up the ice caps?

Glacier ice consists of snow accumulated over decades and centuries. Some snow may melt during summer or warm seasons. But some remains and is covered by more snow falling during the wet seasons. Glacier ice, which makes up the bulk of the white mountain tops, is formed by this process.

There are glaciers on Mt Kenya, Kilimanjaro in northern Tanzania and Rwenzori, on the border between Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

These glaciers have increased and decreased in size during the past centuries and millennia following wetter and drier climatic conditions. The glaciers as features might be as old as 10,000 years, but the ice itself is considerably younger.

The current glacier retreat is unprecedented, outside the range of its natural variation....

item.title: Peace along India-China border essential to development of ties, Modi tells Xi
item.description: The two leaders ‘expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question’.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday said that peace and tranquillity along the India-China border were essential to the continued development of bilateral ties during a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Xi is in India – for the first time in seven years – to attend the BRICS summit. This came amid a thaw since 2024 in India-China relations, following years of tensions over a military standoff in Ladakh.

After their bilateral meeting, Modi and Xi welcomed the “steady progress in India-China bilateral relations” since their last meeting in Tiajin in August 2025, a statement released by the Ministry of External Affairs said.

They also agreed that both countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties and that “differences should not become disputes”.

Modi said the relationship should be guided by three “mutuals”: mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.

The two leaders “expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples”.

item.title: ‘Taipei Story’: Rebecca F Kuang grapples with anxieties of being estranged by and within language
item.description: The novelty of ‘Taipei Story’ is that it seems to be Kuang’s first liaison with comedic writing, which she executes with impeccable timing and taste.
item.content:encoded:
There is no doubt that Rebecca F Kuang is obsessed with language (rightly so). Having recently completed a PhD in East Asian Languages and Literatures at Yale University, she also unpacks questions concerning the linguistic realm through fiction. In an earlier novel, Babel, or the Necessity of Violence (2022), she exposed the role of language in erecting and disrupting structures of power in academic institutions steeped in colonialism. But in her most vulnerable novel yet, Kuang grapples with the anxieties of being estranged by and within language. Taipei Story is an invitation to join in on the madness.

A sociocultural odyssey

The book follows the journey of Chinese-American Ivy League freshman Lily Chen, as she ventures on an intensive (and immersive) Chinese language training programme in Taipei over the summer. Lily, like any child of an immigrant family, has been plagued by the curse of not being American enough and simultaneously constantly failing to be authentically Chinese.

“When I reached my gate at Logan Airport, I discovered there were a lot of Chinese American students boarding the United Flight from Boston to Taipei… They looked Chinese, but not Chinese Chinese… Chinese Americans always looked like Chinese people put through the broiler.”

item.title: BRICS leaders condemn Pahalgam terror attack
item.description: It is the second consecutive year that the multilateral grouping’s declaration has condemned the attack. The joint declaration did not name Pakistan.
item.content:encoded:
The BRICS countries on Saturday condemned the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack and called for combating terrorism in all its forms, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.

It is the second consecutive year that a BRICS leaders’ declaration has condemned the attack. The grouping had also condemned the terror attack that killed 26 persons in its July 2025 declaration issued in Rio de Janeiro.

BRICS comprises India, Brazil, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

Saturday’s declaration did not name Pakistan, which New Delhi has accused of supporting cross-border terrorism. In the past, China has blocked India’s attempts at the United Nations to sanction terror groups based in Pakistan.

In its joint declaration on Saturday, the grouping expressed “strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed”.

The group reiterated that “terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice” under national and international laws.

The BRICS grouping has condemned terrorism in its past declarations too.

item.title: Telangana’s tiger reserve with no tigers
item.description: The Kawal Tiger Reserve connects major tiger landscapes and has large prey populations but no resident big cats.
item.content:encoded:
Deep in northern Telangana, Kawal Tiger Reserve covers a thick forest of teak and bamboo near the Godavari river. Geographically, it sits in an ideal location, connecting major tiger landscapes. It links Tadoba-Andhari in Maharashtra to the west and Indravati in Chhattisgarh to the east. Kawal supports large populations of spotted deer, sambar, nilgai, and wild pigs, alongside leopards and wild dogs. On paper, the tiger reserve checks the boxes of sufficient prey and habitat. But the reserve has no resident tigers.

A 12-year study conducted between 2010 and 2022 confirmed that no tigers live permanently in Kawal. Using systematically placed line transects to monitor prey numbers, researchers found that spotted deer populations grew over the decade, while sambar, nilgai, and chousingha populations remained stable.

Despite this rich prey base, researchers recorded only 15 transient tigers entering Kawal from Maharashtra since 2015. Crucially, only two of these visiting tigers were female. While neighbouring corridors outside the reserve have breeding tigers with cubs, Kawal itself remains empty.

According to lead researcher Imran Siddiqui, this absence comes down to a fundamental difference in how male and female tigers disperse, “Tigers disperse very differently based on sex. Male tigers are bolder risk-takers – they grow faster, leave their mothers earlier,...

item.title: September global nonfiction: Six new titles about humankind’s greatest stories
item.description: Why does Australia not acknowledge its slave trading past? Can AI replace human relationships? Who was Thomas Cochrane, the adventurer?
item.content:encoded:
All information sourced from publishers.

A Dangerous Game: Thomas Cochrane’s Life on the Edge, Peter Moore

The astonishing true story of Thomas Cochrane – naval hero, political radical and inspiration for Patrick O’Brian’s Jack Aubrey – whose audacity at sea, scandals on land and battles across empires make for a tale as thrilling as any novel.

Cochrane’s life was even more remarkable than the fiction it inspired. A hero of the Napoleonic Wars, known for destroying the French Atlantic fleet in one explosive attack, he was an equally aggressive force in British politics as the radical MP for Westminster.

Cochrane’s fortunes turned in 1814, when he was convicted of a fraud on the Stock Exchange. After escaping from prison, he later reinvented himself as a revolutionary admiral, helping the Chileans, Peruvians, Brazilians and Greeks in their struggles for independence.

In A Dangerous Game, historian Peter Moore draws on newly uncovered materials to bring Cochrane vividly to life. Bold, rebellious and uncompromising, he saw the world as a contest to be won – at sea, in politics, even in scandal – and played it more dangerously than any man of his era.

item.description: The Congress has asked the Election Commission to ‘scrutinise’ all poll-related actions taken by Devashish Sharma while he was Nagaon deputy commissioner.
item.content:encoded:
Former Indian Administrative Services officer Devashish Sharma, who took voluntary retirement last week, was on Friday named the Bharatiya Janata Party’s candidate for the Nagaon Lok Sabha bye-poll in Assam on October 6, The Indian Express reported. .

Sharma resigned as Nagaon’s deputy commissioner on September 3 and joined the BJP on Thursday.

A 2011-batch IAS officer of the Assam-Meghalaya cadre, Sharma was appointed deputy commissioner of Nagaon in June 2025, The Indian Express reported. Before taking charge in Nagaon, Sharma served as deputy commissioner of neighbouring Morigaon district, which is also part of the Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency.

The Congress has asked the Election Commission to “review and scrutinise” all the poll-related actions taken by Sharma during his tenure as the deputy commissioner-cum-district election officer, the newspaper reported.

Congress MP Rakibul Hussain wrote to the poll body, raising concerns that Sharma was responsible for electronic voting machines, polling arrangements, staff deployment and implementing Election Commission directives, among other key aspects of the polls in the constituency.

Nagaon, a Muslim-majority constituency in central Assam, has been held by the Congress for the past 10 years. item.title: Uttar Pradesh using Goondas Act as ‘tool of oppression’, says Allahabad HC
item.description: The court said that the act should be used very sparingly in very clear cases of public disorder or for the maintenance of public order.
item.content:encoded:
The Allahabad High Court on Thursday said that the Uttar Pradesh government had continued to use the Goonda Act, meant to control habitual criminals, as a “tool of oppression”, despite the courts’ warnings against its misuse.

Justice Subhash Vidyarthi was hearing a petition by Zahid Ali challenging an order by the Gonda district magistrate declaring him a “goonda” under the 1970 Uttar Pradesh Control of Goondas Act and ordering him to leave the district for six months. The court set aside the order.

“The Goonda Act is a powerful tool for the control and suppression of the ‘Goondas’,” the court said. “It should be used very sparingly in very clear cases of public disorder or for the maintenance of public order.”

It added that the courts have repeatedly held that the act should not be used as a tool to oppress innocent persons and is intended to prevent habitual criminal activity, rather than punish a person without a conviction for a substantial offence.

“The present case is a glaring example of the abuse of the aforesaid statute,” the court said.

The Bombay High Court on Friday refused to issue orders restraining Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange-Patil from holding a march to Mumbai.

“We find at present the entire case of the petitioners is set up on the basis of past experience,” the court said. “There is no such situation as yet which has emerged for us to take cognisance and issue appropriate directions in the matter.”

“State machinery is capable of handling all these situations,” Bar and Bench quoted the court as verbally observing.

Jarange-Patil has been on an indefinite hunger strike in Jalna district since August 29, demanding reservation for the Maratha community under the Other Backward Classes category, The Hindu reported. His demands include the issuance of Kunbi caste certificates to eligible members of the community.

item.title: ‘The River of Grey Flowers’: Good intentions do not always a good novel make
item.description: Rejimon Kuttappan’s novel has its poignant moments, but they are needles in its haystack of digression and awkward prose.
item.content:encoded:
Reading The River of Grey Flowers feels a lot like watching Dhurandhar. While Rejimon Kuttappan’s debut novel has none of Aditya Dhar’s right-wing nationalism, it succumbs to the same fatal flaw in narrative: it depends so much on its events being true stories that it fails to create enough stakes for the characters within its fiction.

The circumstances

Kuttappan is an investigative journalist specialising in migrant rights and forced labour, and this novel borrows from much of the news he has broken. It follows John Easow, a Dalit fisherman’s son, who is a graphic designer by day and turmeric smuggler by night. When he falls in love with Thenmozhi, a savarna woman from the neighbouring village, they marry in secret; he is forced to give up his boat, and therefore his income from smuggling, in exchange for his life. He loses his day job too, and applies to another graphic design role in Dubai – this takes him to Thailand, and then, against his will, to Myawaddy, or Myanmar.

His new role is a forced labour scheme, where he is made to defraud strangers online alongside similarly deceived Dalit and African workers. He poses as different women using different SIM cards, and sweet-talks men into sending him money....

item.title: How India opened a consulate in Odessa – and why it took years
item.description: The mission was meant to serve India’s growing trade with the Soviet Union, but it soon became a hub for sailors, students and cultural exchange.
item.content:encoded:
When Indian foreign service officer PH Desai inaugurated his country’s consulate in Odessa in November 1962, the Black Sea port greeted the milestone with much fanfare. At the time, only three foreign governments maintained diplomatic missions anywhere in the Soviet Union outside Moscow: fellow communist nations Poland and Czechoslovakia operated consulates in Kiev, while Turkey had one in Batumi.

Local journalists covered the opening in a city celebrated for its 19th-century maritime legacy and scarred by fierce fighting during the Second World War. Addressing the press at the opening, Desai noted that three Indian companies maintained regular shipping services between Odessa and Indian ports, while vessels of the Black Sea Shipping Line frequently called at Indian ports.

Odessa carried immense strategic value for New Delhi as the port from where machinery and equipment for the expansion of the Bhilai Steel Plant were shipped to India. In the preceding decade, the absence of an on-the-ground Indian mission had created headaches. Indian merchant seamen frequently attempted to disembark during port calls, leading to tensions, as embassy files from Moscow note, when local authorities refused a few of them entry into the Soviet Union.

Justice Rohit Ranjan Agarwal sought responses from the Uttar Pradesh government and the local administration to a petition by Mohammad Tanveer Ahmad, challenging the eviction proceedings issued to him under the Public Premises Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants Act, 1971.

The mosque was demolished on September 5 following a court’s decision to uphold an earlier order declaring the structure illegal.

Ahmad, however, told the High Court that he had submitted a written statement before a magistrate disputing the claim of illegal construction, and asserted that the mosque had existed on the disputed property for over 100 years, Live Law reported.

Lawyer Ashish Kumar Singh, representing the petitioner, contended that the government had acted hastily in demolishing the mosque, and that the structure was bulldozed within three days of the eviction order.

item.title: Richie Mehta’s film on Phoolan Devi was inspired by ‘a light that shines so bright’
item.description: ‘Phoolan’, led by Sneha Kumari, is being screened at the Toronto International Film Festival.
item.content:encoded:
A gang of dacoits is surrounded in a village by hundreds of policemen. Over 48 hours, the brigands try to escape the siege, relying on their knowledge of the terrain to outwit superior numbers and firepower. Richie Mehta’s new film is a pulsating action thriller but something else too: an extract from the life of the outlaw Phoolan Devi.

Titled Phoolan, the movie from the creator-director of the acclaimed web series Delhi Crime and Poacher is based on an incident from Phoolan Devi: The Autobiography of India’s Bandit Queen, co-authored with Marie-Therese Cuny and Paul Rambali. Written in 1996, years after Phoolan Devi surrendered and served a prison term, the book traces the personal history of brutality – child marriage, repeated rape, discrimination resulting from her Other Backward Caste status – that transformed an impoverished teenager into a feared dacoit in the Chambal ravines.

Phoolan will be premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival (September 10-20). First-time film actor Sneha Kumari plays the lead role. The cast includes Aakash Dahiya, Prateek Pachori and Dev Dutt Budholiya.

Vikram Pratap Singh plays Phoolan Devi’s lover and protector Vikram Mallah (also known as Mastana). Anurag Thakur portrays an unnamed police constable grappling with the moral implications of the siege on the village.

item.title: What is the difference between the Census and National Population Register?
item.description: There are stark variations in the purpose of both exercises. Combining data collection could lead to complications while also raising legal questions.
item.content:encoded:
In 2010, the population enumeration for preparing a National Population Register along with the house listing operations of the Census of 2011, evoked frequent criticism of the NPR. The use of the National Population Register in Assam to prepare the National Register of Citizens wherein everyone had to prove their citizenship contributed to this criticism. In the process, the benefits of an NPR were ignored.

A population register has been defined by the United Nations as, “an individualized data system, that is, a mechanism of continuous recording, and/or of coordinated linkage, of selected information pertaining to each member of the resident population of a country in such a way to provide the possibility of determining up-to-date information concerning the size and characteristics of that population at selected time intervals”.

The United Nations Member States have the responsibility to recognise all individuals present in their territory as a person before the law, without prejudice to nationality (or lack thereof), legal status, gender or duration of stay. The population register must contain all people who are residing in an area.

item.title: ‘Shake off the aura’: Novelist Amitabha Bagchi on originality and borrowing in literary writing
item.description: If an author directly borrows ideas or settings from another author, wrapping them in his own setting and his own style, is that a form of fraud?
item.content:encoded:
As per Umberto Eco, “Books always speak of other books, and every story tells a story that has already been told.” Eco neglected to mention if books only speak of other books, and if it is okay if they do, or should the authors of books that largely speak of other books be hauled over the coals, indicted for their crime and given punishments that are less stringent than those handed out to common plagiarists, but are punishments nonetheless. Had he done so, we wouldn’t have to face the conundrum raised by Urdu novelist Asha’ar Najmi’s long piece (in Hindi) on Khalid Javed’s oeuvre whose thrust is that several of Javed’s wonderfully original-seeming ideas across five novels can be traced back to novelists, thinkers, graphic novelists and filmmakers from the West. The conundrum, stated plainly, is this: What constitutes originality in fiction? item.title: ‘Goa has become internally exotic in India because of its Portuguese heritage’
item.description: An interview with R Benedito Ferrão, author of ‘Across Continents: Writing Goans, Making Worlds.’
item.content:encoded:
Goans have moved across continents for centuries, travelling as Portuguese nationals through British colonies, building communities in East Africa, navigating citizenship regimes that could not decide whether they were Indian, European, or something else entirely. R Benedito Ferrão’s Across Continents: Writing Goans, Making Worlds examines what happens when that experience enters fiction. Published in Michigan University Press’s African Perspectives series, the book reads Goan characters across four novels connected to different continents: Salman Rushdie’s Midnight’s Children, MG Vassanji’s The Book of Secrets, Roger King’s A Girl from Zanzibar, and Margaret Mascarenhas’s Skin, bringing paintings, etchings, and pop music into dialogue with the literary texts to surface what prose alone leaves buried.

Ferrão is an Associate Professor of English and Asian and Pacific Islander American Studies at William & Mary, Virginia, US. Additionally, he is the Dr Thomas Tam Visiting Professor of Asian American Studies at the City University of New York’s Asian American/Asian Research Institute. His previous publications include the edited volume Goa, Portugal, Mozambique: The Many Lives of Vamona Navelcar, which accompanied an exhibition he curated at Fundação Oriente in Goa, and the co-published The Girl Who was the Color of Nothing: A Children’s Story for Adults with the artist, Maria Vanessa de Sa, who also created the cover image for Across Continents.

item.title: Size matters: Why India has a stake in the Africa-led campaign to decolonise world maps
item.description: The Mercator map that is now most familiar distorts the size of Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania and inflates landmasses towards the poles.
item.content:encoded:
Maps are supposed to tell us what the world looks like – the names, shapes and sizes of landmasses and water bodies. Though they are considered neutral depictions of land and sea, they can be sites of contention. Nations sometimes vie with one another to imprint their vision on how the landmasses they occupy, or wish to occupy, are perceived.

The map of the world that is most familiar to us is the Mercator map from the sixteenth century, named for the Flemish cartographer who created it. It has shaped our view of the world and, despite its well-known distortions, is widely used.

The Mercator map is inaccurate because it distorts the size and landmass of Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania and inflates landmasses towards the poles. For example, Africa and Greenland appear to be roughly the same size, when in reality Africa is approximately 14 times larger than Greenland.

In fact, Africa is approximately 30.3 sq million – larger than the United States, China, India and much of Europe combined.

Not surprisingly, Southern nations support movements that demand equal-area geographic representations that challenge the dominant Eurocentric size distortions. The most successful campaign to date is the “Correct the Map” campaign.

item.title: Why Kenya’s universal health reform is contentious
item.description: All Kenyans are now expected to register with the new Social Health Authority and contribute 2.75% of their income.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Kenyans without health insurance have had one option when they fall sick, or a hospital bill arrives. Reach out to friends and family to gather what they can for their healthcare.

By 2023, official figures showed only about a quarter of Kenyans had any health cover. And most of these were people working in formal sector jobs. For the remaining 75%, who had no cover, falling sick meant paying out of their own pockets at health facilities. The few exceptions include maternity care and basic services in local clinics.

The World Health Organization estimates that half of all people worldwide impoverished by out-of-pocket health expenditures live in Africa.

In 2023, shortly after taking office, President William Ruto’s government pushed through a major health financing law, the Social Health Insurance Act. This new law scrapped the National Hospital Insurance Fund, the state insurer since 1966. The insurer had collected members’ contributions and paid their hospital bills, yet only managed to cover about a quarter of Kenyans. The new law replaced it with a new body, the Social Health Authority.

item.title: Parties skipped disclosing details of 191 candidates with criminal cases in 2026 polls: Study
item.description: The Supreme Court requires parties to explain why they chose candidates with criminal cases over those without.
item.content:encoded:

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Hymns for Longing’, by Agnibarathi.
item.content:encoded:
Hymn for Awakening

My mind is a bird
with a forked tail
fighting foes
greater than me.

I rise at dawn
and twirl and fight,
stir the overrun milk
of the day and cry in alarm.
My voice, it dons
many a cloak,
all but my own.

Pierce me, my love
with your sunbeam’s spear.
Plunder my vain clinking trinkets.

Return to me, my love,
my very own silence
and let me gaze unblinking
at your blinding glory.


Hymn for Hunting

Unwavering, my heart,
like a shikra circling distant skies
with fiery eye fixed on obscure prey
pursues you,
only you, my love.

Your waist, my love,
like a serpent that in itself
brews venom from birth and
spends it all in a single strike,
brews eternal nectar for my moment’s yen.

Like spears that fly
drawn to their foes,

like milk that flows
drawn to calves,

like seas in tumult
drawn to clouds,

my deeds, your dreams
entwined are drawn,

to death, to desire,
to us,
my love.


The Churning of a Moment’s Pleasure

Come.
Sit in my lap.
Now are our bodies one mythic mountain.

Hold.
Clasp my arms.
Now are our limbs, one cosmic serpent.

Sink.
Then rise afloat.
Now am I the turtle holding your world.

Churn. Churn. Churn.
Your gods. My demons.
My gods. Your demons.

First comes venom.

Swallow.
Hold it in our throats.
Now are we hung between life and death.

Next come treasures.

Split.
You take wealth. I take boons.
Now are we insolvent debtors forever.

At last from the shimmering ocean,
when demons become gods,
when gods become immortal, and
god becomes a seductress,

comes

nectar, nectar, nectar.

Spill.
Let life overflow and lavish.
Now have we wasted an eternity for

a moment’s pleasure.


Gossiping with a god

This afternoon,
cloistered by the bleak monsoon clouds
I invite the dancing Siva to gossip.

At my call,
he relaxes, his rigidly fluid pose,
lets the river of his hair ramble,
casts off his cool crescent moon,
lays aside his fire of wisdom,
frees the demon of ignorance,
and sits ungainly on my couch.

item.title: The 9/11 New York attacks prompted an over-reliance on security technology – leaving us vulnerable
item.description: Surveillance systems are routinely overhyped, with benefits assumed and failures routinely overlooked.
item.content:encoded:
It has been 25 years since the devastating attacks of September 11, 2001. Amid the reflection that followed emerged the most comprehensive examination of any terrorist attack in history, the 9/11 Commission Report. Several statements in this forensic diagnosis continue to shape our understanding of those events. These range from the intelligence systems that were “blinking red” in the months preceding the attacks to various institutional “failures of imagination” that left the threat unrecognised.

Yet the commission’s investigation into the circumstances of the 9/11 terrorist attacks was also, fundamentally, a report on how to reimagine and improve security. The commission’s recommendations foreshadowed and legitimised a new model of security that emerged from the ashes of the twin towers, one centred on protecting critical infrastructure using an integrated security architecture.

The 9/11 commission’s blueprint involved integrating agencies, systems and technologies. This principle took many forms. The integration of intelligence reporting is illustrated by UK’s Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre. Technology became weaved into security activities. Important spaces were fortified using a “layered security” approach.

Symbolic buildings, financial districts, city centres, stadiums, high-end shopping malls, and especially airports were the first to be upgraded. item.title: Why has India’s G20 fanfare not been replicated for BRICS summit?
item.description: The limits of reproducing diplomatic spectacle indefinitely are becoming clear.
item.content:encoded:
When world leaders gathered in New Delhi for the G20 Summit in September 2023, the spectacle surrounding the event was impossible to miss. Under the chairmanship of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the summit was celebrated as India’s grand arrival on the global stage. Streets were lined with banners, cultural motifs saturated the summit’s visual landscape, and official messaging projected India as the “voice of the Global South”.

Three years later, India is preparing to host the 2026 summit of BRICS, but there is a palpable contrast. Unlike the build-up to the G20, there is little of the expansive public mobilisation, symbolic messaging, or political fanfare that characterised 2023. Meanwhile, uncertainty continues to surround the summit-level meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, commonly known as the “Quad,” which was expected to take place in India this year.

At the same time, New Delhi has stepped back from hosting the 33rd Conference of Parties under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in 2028, despite having earlier expressed willingness to do so. These developments suggest a more selective approach to international summitry that is shaped by altered geopolitical circumstances and the limits of reproducing diplomatic spectacle indefinitely.

item.title: How Sweden went from asylum haven to enacting Europe’s strictest migration policies
item.description: The political consensus that emerged in little under a decade is for the country to maintain restrictive migration policies.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Sweden was known as one of Europe’s most welcoming countries for refugees. It took pride in pursuing one of Europe’s most generous asylum policies, and often presented itself as a humanitarian role model.

But today it has one of the continent’s most restrictive migration policies. That transformation has taken little more than a decade.

The turning point came during the 2015 refugee crisis. Sweden received more than 160,000 asylum applications, more than 12% of all applications in the European Union. Around 35,000 were unaccompanied minors, more than one third of the EU total that year. The scale of the inflow exposed strains on the country’s system and fundamentally changed the political debate around migration.

The immediate response was a broad cross-party agreement introducing stricter asylum and family migration rules. This was followed by temporary border controls, and the replacement of permanent residence permits with temporary ones for most refugees.

These measures, introduced by a leftwing Social Democratic government, were more than a response to an exceptional situation. They signalled the emergence of a new political consensus: that Sweden should pursue a substantially more restrictive migration policy.

Aarti Rawal* is a 27-year-old resident of Delhi. In 2025 for the first time, Rawal took the flu vaccine on her doctor’s recommendation, “after a spell of long Covid in 2023 and 2024 messed up my health”, she said. “I’d get recurrent bronchial attacks exacerbated by winter pollution.”

When she repeated the shot in spring this year, she got her family to take it as well, even though they showed some reluctance. “They didn’t think it was necessary,” said Rawal.

item.title: How Ahmedabad became an unwelcoming city

In 1972, community organiser Ela Bhatt and a group of women met at Ahmedabad’s Victoria Garden to discuss the conditions in which self-employed women worked. That meeting led to the formation of the Self-Employed Women’s Association, or SEWA, which became one of India’s most significant labour organisations.

Ahmedabad’s public spaces have never just been places to pass the time: since the freedom struggle, they have hosted many important gatherings meant to organise, debate and build political movements.

A group of people had gathered to read books including Anne Frank’s diary, Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala, Bhagat Singh’s Why I Am an Atheist and George Orwell’s 1984. The organisation later said its objection was directed at Yousafzai, citing her views on Pakistan and Kashmir. item.title: Behind deaths of Adivasi children in Balaghat: appalling vaccination levels, widespread hunger

In June, one-year-old Sahil caught a fever and developed a rash all over his body. A month later, he was dead, mostly likely from a measles-malaria outbreak that ripped through Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district.

Sahil’s 12-year-old sister Lamnin fell ill with similar symptoms and died a day later at their home in Bondari village.

As Scroll reported in the first part of this series, at least 25 children from the Baiga and Gond tribes have died since May in this remote Adivasi habitation in Madhya Pradesh. For two months, the outbreak went undetected because of the complete absence of a healthcare system in the area.

Measles is a disease that can be prevented through vaccination. India added the measles vaccine to its universal immunisation programme in 1985.

But four decades later, in the villages of Balaghat, we found that immunisation drives against measles existed only on paper.

item.title: William T Vollmann has written a 3,000‑page novel when the world appears to be done with big books
item.description: Vollmann’s new novel, ‘A Table for Fortune’, explores what happens when the response to the horrors of 9/11 becomes an arena for perpetration of more crimes.
item.content:encoded:
With forecasters of doom debating the end of reading, of publishing and of literacy in general, what should we make of William T Vollmann’s forthcoming novel, A Table for Fortune?

Spanning four volumes at 3,000 pages, is it madness? A determined attempt to silence print’s naysayers?

I have been writing about Vollmann’s works since I penned the introduction to “William T Vollmann: A Critical Companion” more than 10 years ago.

The 67-year-old author has spent his career going big, in every sense, and I would not be the first to describe his approach to his art as uncompromising.

His projects grapple with weighty matters such as global poverty, the history of North America and climate change. Few of his roughly 25 books run under 500 pages. About half try to keep his readers engaged for several hundred pages beyond that. Many of them supplement the text with photographs, epigraphs, glossaries, family trees, sketches, timelines, variant tables of contents, alternating fonts and notes to the reader. The essay “Rising Up and Rising Down,” his philosophical and journalistic inquiry into the nature of violence, clocks in at over 3,000 pages across seven volumes.

item.title: Nepal floods halt contentious hydropower exports to Bangladesh via India
item.description: The disruption comes amid load-shedding in Bangladesh and a few months after an Indian power trading company declined Nepal’s request to export 20 MW more.
item.content:encoded:
Monsoon rains have routinely given Nepal a surge of hydropower, creating a surplus. Some of that surplus was used to supplement downstream neighbour Bangladesh’s fossil-fuel-dependent electricity supply.

On August 2, however, Nepal’s hydropower system was damaged extensively. Flash floods swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems, killing at least 1,250 people as of 3 September. The floods also damaged 15 hydropower plants and critical transmission infrastructure, wiping out over 750 MW of electricity generation, reported Time. Nearly 900 hydropower workers are missing.

The disaster has now disrupted Nepal’s electricity exports, with supplies to Bangladesh halted, authorities in Dhaka and Kathmandu confirmed to Dialogue Earth.

On September 3, Shaligram Bhandari, a spokesperson for Nepal’s Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, told Dialogue Earth that floods damaged the 22 megawatt Chilime and 24 MW Trishuli hydropower projects, which have since stopped generating electricity. The power they produced had been approved for export to Bangladesh. Nepal halted all power exports, Reuters reported several days earlier.

Amid the disaster, the ministry had yet to explore alternatives, Bhandari said. Nepal’s growing role as a hydropower exporter must be viewed together with these vulnerabilities.

On August 19, the bench had given the Odisha Sentence Review Board a final opportunity and verbally stated that the court would take the decision in the matter if the state failed to do so by the next hearing.

However, counsel for the Odisha government on Tuesday sought a four-week adjournment, citing the illness of its advocate-on-record, the legal news outlet reported.

Staines and his minor sons were burnt to death by a mob led by Singh in Odisha in January 1999 when they were sleeping in a jeep. The attackers had accused the missionary of illegal religious conversion.

Sudhanshu, who ran the “Hostel Daze” paying guest accommodation, is being questioned after his arrest, the news agency quoted unidentified officials as saying. He and his business partner, Shubham Tyagi, had leased the property from its owner in August 2025. Tyagi is absconding.

Sudhanshu’s arrest is the fifth in the case. The building’s owner, Hari Ram, his son Mahesh, his wife Urmila and labour contractor Saroj were arrested earlier, The Indian Express reported.

item.title: ‘It could kill us all’: Anthropic researcher quits over AI safety concerns
item.description: The artificial intelligence industry was ‘racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives’, Jacob Coxon said on social media.
item.content:encoded:
A researcher at artificial intelligence company Anthropic has quit, claiming that he is concerned that the firm and the industry are racing to build AI systems that he believes they will not be able to control.

In a series of social media posts on Wednesday, Jacob Coxon said that he had done pre-training research at United States-based firms Anthropic and OpenAI for the past three years, and that “neither company is acting responsibly”. The firms were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”, he said.

In AI, “pre-training” refers to the initial phase where a machine learning model learns patterns, grammar, facts and structures from a dataset before it can be trained for specific tasks.

In a series of social media posts, Coxon said that people should not underestimate the power of artificial intelligence.

“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” he said. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Anthropic has not yet commented on Coxon’s resignation, or on the concerns he raised.

item.title: Instagram accounts of three journalists reporting on MP child deaths briefly suspended
item.description: While the accounts were later restored, the Press Club of India said the matter raised concerns about attempts to intimidate or silence journalists.

Instagram on Monday briefly suspended the accounts of three independent journalists who had been reporting on the deaths of Adivasi children in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district. The accounts were back online on Wednesday morning.

The Instagram accounts of Monika Singh, Bindu Gurjar and Lokbhadra Singh had been suspended by the social media platform. All three had been reporting on protests by Adivasi groups following the deaths of the children, highlighting hospital mismanagement and the struggles of ASHA workers in the region, among other subjects.

After his account was restored, Lokbhadra Singh alleged that attempts were being made to “harass the journalists and break their spirit”, but that they would not back down.

Earlier this month, Scroll reported that a mysterious measles and malaria outbreak in the region went undetected for at least two months, and led to the deaths of at least 25 children from the Baiga and Gond tribes.

item.title: Instead of chasing GDP growth, India must redesign its broken ladder of upward mobility
item.description: Young Indians only want gainful employment to secure their future. The economy has simply not delivered on that.
item.content:encoded:
India’s leaders must find systemic solutions to the country’s employment problems. The economy is not creating enough good jobs for young people, even if more were to pursue higher education and the examination system functioned smoothly. More technology to fix the examination system will not solve the deeper problem of the economy.

Moreover, there is increasing evidence that use of more technology and AI will worsen India’s unemployment crisis. While it may be unclear whether AI will create more jobs ultimately, it is sufficiently clear that inequality will rise during the transition, increasing further the distance between “haves” and “have nots”.

India’s youth need a ladder to climb to reach their aspirations. They want gainful employment, and to earn enough to secure their own and their families’ futures. They are married on a cold September day in 1963 in London. My father arrived a year or two earlier from Kenya, which he left in the months during the run-up to Kenyan independence – the second independence movement he would witness in his life. The Indian state of Punjab, where he was born, was almost exclusively agricultural at the time, its economy fundamentally entwined with the soil and seasons.

The family owned a small portion of land, divided, as far as I know, between my grandfather and his two brothers. item.title: Why an old demand to release Sikh prisoners is gathering political force in Punjab
item.description: The call to release nine prisoners still in jail has become a rallying cry for new political outfits in Punjab who are championing Panthic issues.
item.content:encoded:
On August 21, several cities of Punjab woke up to a complete shutdown in support of a call to release Sikh convicts lodged in different jails across the country.

Popularly called “Bandi Singhs”, the prisoners were convicted and sentenced by different courts for their involvement in the Punjab militancy during the 1980s and 1990s. Some of them are serving life sentences.

The call for a statewide shutdown had come from Qaumi Insaaf Morcha, a Sikh advocacy group that has fought for the release of the prisoners for decades.

At the centre of the Morcha’s agitation is Jagtar Singh Hawara, a man convicted for the assassination of Punjab Chief Minister Beant Singh.

Hawara and Balwant Singh Rajoana, both members of the banned militant group Babbar Khalsa, were sentenced to death by a trial court in 2007 for carrying out a bomb blast outside the Punjab Civil Secretariat in Chandigarh in 1995. Along with the chief minister, the blast had also killed 16 people. Hawara’s sentence was later commuted to imprisonment for life.

The Qaumi Insaaf Morcha is seeking a four-week parole for Hawara. “His mother is 81 and suffering from Alzheimer’s,” said Gursharan Singh Dhaliwal, Hawara’s lawyer. “We are seeking parole in order to allow a son to meet his mother.”
